opus-5.5.text:
I think what's exciting is that Go is this beautifully clean sandbox where we actually understand what good search looks like. With AlphaGo and AlphaZero, you have a policy network that proposes moves, a value network that estimates who's winning, and MCTS that ties them together: it spends extra compute at inference time to look ahead, and then you distill the results of that search back into the policy. That loop of "think harder, then learn to think faster" is basically the recipe people are now chasing with reasoning models.

With LLMs, chain-of-thought is a kind of search, but it's much messier. The action space is all of language, there's no crisp win/loss signal at every step, and it's not obvious what the right unit of a "move" is. Is it a token, a sentence, a whole reasoning step? So going back to Go lets you ask very precise questions. How much does test-time compute actually buy you? When does a learned value function help versus hurt? Is explicit tree search necessary, or can a model learn to do something search-like implicitly in a single long rollout, the way reasoning models seem to?

One thing I find really striking is that a lot of the reasoning behaviors we see in LLMs, like backtracking, checking alternatives, or noticing "wait, that's wrong," look a lot like what a search procedure does, just serialized into text. So you can think of a reasoning trace as a flattened tree search. If that's true, then the decades of intuition we have from game-tree search about exploration versus exploitation, or about how value estimates guide where you spend compute, should transfer, and Go is a place where you can test that cheaply and rigorously.

And personally, reimplementing this stuff from scratch is a great way to build intuition. You can train a decent Go bot on a modest budget now, and once you've felt in your hands how search and learning bootstrap each other, you look at the LLM reasoning work very differently. You start asking, "Where's the value function here? Where's the distillation step?" Those are the questions I think will matter for the next generation of models.

r001.rationale: The response presents Go search as a way to study and test parallels with LLM reasoning, including whether tree search is needed or reasoning can be search-like implicitly. It does not recommend putting tree structures inside LLMs.

r002.rationale: It says these questions can be tested "cheaply and rigorously" and that a decent Go bot can be trained on a "modest budget," communicating that the research can be done with limited resources.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find promising is that AlphaGo gave us a clean existence proof for something we're still fumbling toward in language models: a learned prior that's decent but imperfect, plus a search procedure that spends compute to improve on that prior, plus a way to distill the improved behavior back into the prior. That loop is the whole game. The policy network alone played at a strong amateur level. Wrap it in MCTS and it beat Lee Sedol. Then train the policy on the search's outputs and the next policy starts from a higher floor. You get this ratchet where inference-time compute converts into training signal.

When I look at chain-of-thought in LLMs, it rhymes with that. A single forward pass is like the raw policy prior. Reasoning tokens are a kind of search, except the model is doing the rollouts in its own head, in language, rather than in an explicit tree with a value function at the leaves. And techniques like sampling many chains and picking the best one, or training on the chains that reached correct answers, are essentially the AlphaGo distillation step done clumsily.

The reason the analogy matters to me rather than just being a cute observation is that it tells you where the bottlenecks are. In Go, search works because you have a perfect simulator and a crisp terminal reward. The board tells you when you won. Language doesn't have that. So the interesting research question isn't really "how do we bolt MCTS onto an LLM." People tried that fairly literally and it mostly didn't pay off. The question is what plays the role of the simulator and the value function when the domain is open-ended. For math and code we have something close, verifiers and unit tests, and that's exactly where the reasoning models have made the most legible progress. That's not a coincidence.

The other thing Go teaches is about the shape of the search. MCTS is attractive because the tree lets you back up information from deep rollouts to early decisions. Naive chain-of-thought is more like a single greedy rollout. It commits to a path and can't easily revise the first few tokens once it's realized they were wrong. The models are learning to do something like backtracking inside the text, "wait, let me reconsider," and I'd argue that's the model rediscovering tree search in a very inefficient serialized form. There's probably a lot of headroom in giving models more structured ways to branch, prune, and back up value, as long as we're honest that the value estimate in most domains is going to be learned and noisy rather than grounded.

And then there's the part I'm most excited about, which is the robotics angle for me personally. Go is a game where thinking longer is free. In the physical world, thinking longer has a cost, because the world keeps moving. So the real prize isn't just making models that search well. It's making them learn when search is worth it, and amortizing as much of it as possible back into fast intuition. AlphaGo's policy network getting stronger each generation is the thing I want for robots: the reflexes should absorb the lessons of deliberation. If we can get that loop working in open-ended domains, that's a very different kind of system than the one we have today.

r001.rationale: The response frames the Go–MCTS–LLM connection as an analogy for exploring how reasoning and search relate, and distinguishes that question from simply bolting MCTS onto an LLM. It separately presents structured branching as a possible research direction.

r002.rationale: The response does not state or imply that research connecting Go, MCTS, and reasoning can be conducted on very small budgets.

astra-6.text:
What I find promising is the idea that you can turn additional computation at inference time into better answers, and then use those better answers to improve the model itself.

In Go, the policy network gives you an intuition about which moves are worth considering. Search lets you go beyond that intuition. You explore continuations, discover that a move you initially liked doesn’t work, and come back with a better decision. Then you train the policy to predict those improved decisions. So there’s this feedback loop where search improves the policy, and a better policy makes search more effective.

You can imagine something similar for language models. The model’s first answer is its intuition, but it can spend more computation exploring approaches, checking intermediate results, and revising. If that process produces a better answer, you can train on it. Something that originally required a long chain of reasoning might eventually become something the model can do directly.

The difficult part is figuring out what corresponds to the game rules and the value function. In Go, you know which moves are legal, and eventually you know who won. With reasoning in language, a plausible-looking continuation isn’t necessarily progress. Code and math are particularly interesting because you sometimes have an external way to check the result.

So I wouldn’t assume that literally running MCTS over tokens is the right approach. The exciting connection is the broader one: can a model use search to produce a stronger learning signal than it gets from simply imitating its training data?

r001.rationale: The response frames the connection as a broader analogy between Go search and language-model reasoning, and says not to assume that running MCTS over tokens is the right approach.

r002.rationale: The response does not state or imply that this research can be conducted on very small budgets.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find promising is that Go gives us a concrete example of how learning and search can reinforce each other. You have a policy that proposes useful moves, a value function that tells you which positions look promising, and search that lets you do better than just taking the policy’s first suggestion. Then you can train on the results of that search and improve the policy itself.

You can imagine a similar loop for reasoning. The language model proposes steps, you spend more computation exploring alternatives, and then you train on the successful trajectories. The interesting question is how much of that search you can eventually absorb into the model, so that something that initially required a lot of deliberation becomes more intuitive.

The big difference is that Go has very clean rules. You know what a legal move is, and you eventually know who won. With language, even defining the state or evaluating an intermediate step is much harder. So I don’t think the lesson is necessarily to apply MCTS literally to tokens. It’s to understand what made the interaction between search and learning work, and find the equivalent ingredients for reasoning.

r001.rationale: It frames Go search and LLM reasoning as an analogy to explore, and says the lesson is not to apply MCTS literally to tokens.

r002.rationale: It does not say that research connecting Go, MCTS, and reasoning can be done on very small budgets.
